device-residency.name: device residency
device-residency.definition: Keeping tensors in GPU-accessible memory across a sequence of dependent operations.
device-residency.explanation: Device residency avoids copying parameters, activations, and gradients through the CPU after every kernel. In the reference project, inputs and parameters are uploaded once; forward writes logits and hidden activations, backward consumes them and writes gradients, and update changes the same parameter buffer. Only final parameters and a loss history are read back. Residency is necessary for efficient GPU training, though this tiny demonstration still uses a serial gradient kernel and host-recorded steps.

forward-kernel.name: forward kernel
forward-kernel.definition: A GPU compute stage that evaluates activations and logits from inputs and current parameters.
forward-kernel.explanation: Each forward invocation owns one training example. It reads two input features, evaluates four tanh hidden units, stores those activations for backward, and computes one output logit. The kernel does not update parameters. It mirrors the scalar model's forward operation, while probability applies sigmoid for the task output. Keeping forward separate makes its data dependencies visible: backward must see complete activations from the same parameter version, so the host records a pass boundary before launching backward.

backward-kernel.name: backward kernel
backward-kernel.definition: A GPU compute stage that applies the chain rule to produce parameter gradients.
backward-kernel.explanation: The backward kernel starts from the output derivative p − y, propagates it through output weights and tanh derivatives, and accumulates all seventeen parameter gradients. It also accumulates the same stable binary cross-entropy as the scalar model. Both loss and gradient divide by the full eight-example batch size. The teaching implementation uses one invocation so the summation is deterministic and easy to compare with the CPU oracle. A scalable version would reduce private partial gradients.

kernel-ordering.name: kernel ordering
kernel-ordering.definition: The command sequence that ensures a consumer stage sees a producer stage's completed writes.
kernel-ordering.explanation: A workgroup barrier orders lanes only within one workgroup and one dispatch. It cannot order the forward kernel against backward or update. The host records these as separate compute passes in one command encoder: forward, then backward, then update. The queue executes that submitted command buffer in order. Reversing update and backward would mutate parameters before gradients using the old forward activations were complete, breaking the derived algorithm.
